newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA COMMUNIST SLOGANS OUTLIVE POLITICAL CHANGE.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA COMMUNIST SLOGANS OUTLIVE POLITICAL CHANGE.

text.p: As politicians open their campaigns for next month's general election, Bulgarians say the slogans aren't what they used to be.

During 45 years of communist rule, rousing messages were virtually everywhere -- on buildings, along highways, in schools and each director's office, as ubiquitous as the red star and the hammer and sickle.
Serious issues of political and economic reform are at stake for the April 19 election, and parties' campaign slogans no longer display the inadvertent surrealism of their totalitarian predecessors.

Mottoes like "every tomato -- a nail in the coffin of imperialism", which promoted food growing, were dreamed up by the ideological department of the Communist Party Central Committee or by local party functionaries.
Sofia citizens still recall one at the Sofia circus big top which is said to have read "35 years of people's power in Bulgaria, 35 years of circus".
Hristo Milkov, historian at the Bulgarian Academy of Science, said the slogan had been an attempt to give the communists the credit for Bulgaria's award-winning acrobats.

"Bulgaria is world famous for the skills of its circus artistes, and the slogans had to convince people that everything that was worthy has been established or reached its peak under socialism," he said.

Milkov, who has spent years collecting slogans and has written an academic thesis on them, said they were a result of serious work of writers, sociologists and party functionaries aimed at strengthening the grip of the party on people's minds.
"The communist slogans seemed like a joke, but it was a dangerous joke as they were part of the overall mechanism aimed at keeping the communist regime in power," he said.
SLOGANS REFLECT RISING AND FALLING STARS
Posters of smiling party leaders, waving to crowds or pointing towards the bright communist future, and quotations from their rousing speeches were everywhere.

One slogan borrowed from a song dedicated to the Soviet, Yugoslav and Bulgarian Communist leaders started out as "Stalin, Tito, Dimitrov, three stars who shine forever, three hearts to beat together". It went through several revisions as Stalin became discredited and Tito cut his links with Moscow.
"Each time when the Party changed its relations to one of these leaders his name and his 'star in the sky' had to be replaced by another one in the respective party," Milkov said.
He said no matter how meaningless some of the slogans were, they were historically important as a reflection of the time.
"They are a reliable source for the events as they are created with a certain aim at a certain moment of history and reflect the point of view of a certain political force."

The Bulgarian Communist Party traces its roots back to 1891 and retains its allegiance to Georgi Dimitrov, one of the leaders of the anti-fascist resistance when Bulgaria was allied to the Axis powers during World War Two.

After 1944 Bulgaria became the Soviet Union's closest ally and regarded Moscow as its "Big Brother", a view reflected in slogans like one which hung in hospitals and read: "Soviet patients are the least ill in the world".

Lyuben Dilov, producer of the popular satirical television show Kanaleto whose sketches often make ironic comparisons between the privations of the past and the present, said his favourite communist slogans were from the period of agricultural reform in the 1970s.
"Each agricultural cooperative -- a blow against the enemies of communism" and "A cow for every home" are just two which he said "illustrated the absurdity of that time".
LONG LIVE THE INTERNATIONAL SITUATION

"During that time the slogans were a constant part of people's lives, hanging everywhere as a sign that the construction of communism was under way...regardless of the results," recalls pensioner Tsveta Dimitrova.
"But at a time when nobody dared to laugh openly at the communist rulers, it was amusing to see slogans like that which showed how narrow-minded the party functionaries were."

She said there was one popular motto which sounded very humane -- "Everything for the man" -- but in real life "the man" usually turned out to be a prominent party leader with a villa on the Black Sea coast and a brand new Mercedes.

Former communist leader Todor Zhivkov was convicted in 1992 of embezzling 21.5 million levs (then about $24 million) of public funds, spent on luxury apartments and Western cars for his family and aides.
The Supreme Court overturned the sentence last year but he remains under house arrest on separate charges.
After the collapse of one-party rule, most former communists resurfaced in the Bulgarian Socialist Party, which won a clear majority in the 1994 general election.
They lost support as economic crisis deepened and were ousted last month after 30 days of mass street protests led by the anti-communist Union of Democratic Forces (UDF).

The opening of the Socialists' campaign showed the leftist slogans were still alive. The party's mainly elderly supporters carried banners which said "No to destabilisation of the country" and "Yes to agricultural cooperatives".
The UDF have slogans of their own, mostly celebrating their victory over the communists in 1989 and the Socialists in 1997.
But Bulgarians retain affection for the sheer oddness of a banner which used to hang across the Sofia-Plovdiv highway which said simply: "Long live the international situation".
